title: Velocity along the motion
spoken: The velocity along x in the moving system is the velocity along x in the stationary system minus the speed of the moving system, divided by one minus that speed times the stationary velocity along x over the speed of light squared.
explanation: Speeds do not simply subtract. An object moving at 15/17 of c in the stationary system moves at 0.6c in a system that itself moves at 0.6c; light, u_x = c, moves at c in both.
assumptions: The moving system moves along x at speed v relative to the stationary system, with |v| < c; the object moves at velocity (u_x, u_y) in the stationary system.
Modern teaching notation: gamma is the paper's beta, c its V. The paper composes speeds the other way round, from the moving system to the stationary one; this is the same relation inverted.

notes.title: One minus v u_x over c squared
notes.explanation: Close to 1 at everyday speeds, which is why speeds seem simply to subtract.

notes.title: c squared
notes.explanation: The square of the speed of light.

notes.title: v u_x over c squared
notes.explanation: The correction Galilean subtraction leaves out.

notes.title: u_x minus v
notes.explanation: The Galilean answer, what subtraction alone would give.

notes.title: Divided by the correction
notes.explanation: Dividing by a number below 1 raises the result, and it can never pass c.

notes.title: What it asserts
notes.explanation: The velocity along x one system assigns, from the velocity the other assigns. For u_x = c the result is c.

notes.title: Speed of the moving system
notes.explanation: Along x. Its sign gives the direction.

notes.title: Speed of the moving system
notes.explanation: Along x. Its sign gives the direction.

notes.title: Velocity along x, stationary system
notes.explanation: The object's velocity along the motion, in the stationary system.
